findings.section: FAQ quick-fire, FAQ 2
findings.quote: **FAQ 2.** Can data leave EFS IA early without a charge? ... Yes: [no minimum storage duration](../facts/efs.md#efs-faq-archive-minimum-duration-90-days).
findings.evidence: Fact efs-faq-archive-minimum-duration-90-days (www/efs/faq) says only 'EFS IA has no minimum storage duration.' It says nothing about a charge-free exit. The chapter itself says the opposite for reads: fact efs-ia-archive-billed-per-class-plus-access-charges ('billed data access charges', used in the lifecycle section 'Why not move everything?'), and speak item s04 must_not_say 'Cold storage is free to read.' A reader who skims 'leave EFS IA early without a charge? Yes' learns that moving or reading IA data is free. Reword the question to what the quote supports, for example 'Does EFS IA charge for deleting a file early?' or 'Does EFS IA have a minimum storage duration?'.
findings.resolution: fix-23: Same fix as claims-23-02.

findings.section: Elastic throughput follows the workload and Provisioned throughput follows your setting, table
findings.quote: | Runs at [5% or more of the average-to-peak ratio](../facts/efs.md#efs-provisioned-use-when-known-needs-5-percent-or-more) | Provisioned |
findings.evidence: STYLE plain English; READER: 'Headings, tables and captions must give a correct gist on their own.' 'Runs at 5% or more of the ... ratio' does not say what is measured, and the two rows overlap at exactly 5% (Elastic: '5% or less', Provisioned: '5% or more'). She cannot apply this table to a stem. Fact efs-provisioned-use-when-known-needs-5-percent-or-more also gives the first and more useful condition, 'if you know your workload's performance requirements', which the table leaves out. Add a column 'Average throughput compared with peak' with plain values ('low: 5% of peak or less' / 'steady: above that'), and add the 'known requirements' condition to the Provisioned row.
findings.resolution: fix-23: Table header is now 'Average throughput compared with peak'; rows 'Low or spiky: 5% or less of the peak throughput' and 'Steady: 5% or more of the average-to-peak ratio, or you know your workload's performance requirements'.

findings.section: Elastic throughput follows the workload and Provisioned throughput follows your setting, Stop and answer
findings.quote: A 50 GiB file system serves a nightly job that reads at a steady high rate and runs out of burst credits. Which mode fits?
findings.evidence: The term 'burst credits' appears here and in the stem of efs-fsx-q003 ('has used all of its burst credits'), but the chapter never explains it. Bursting is described only as 'scales with the amount of storage'. The mechanism, cause and effect, is missing: a small file system earns a low baseline, and a long steady load uses up the credits, so throughput drops. Without it, the Stop and answer and q003 test a word she has not read. Add one sentence with a fact link (the efs.jsonl canon has Bursting facts such as efs-throughput-bursting-scales-with-storage and efs-throughput-bursting-constrained-move-to-elastic-or-provisioned), or add 'burst credit' to the terms of the chapter.
findings.resolution: fix-23: Bursting step now: 'It spends burst credits, deducted when throughput exceeds the base rate' (efs-bursting-credits-accrue-below-base-and-deducted-above).

findings.section: Cold files move to cheaper classes and stay there unless you ask, Try it
findings.quote: > **Try it:** Set a lifecycle policy and see which throughput change it blocks. See [3-do.md](3-do.md). <!-- task: efs-fsx-t02 -->
findings.evidence: The section never says that a lifecycle policy can block a throughput change. The rule is only in task t02 (explain), in speak s04 (follow-up) and nowhere in the prose: fact efs-archive-needs-elastic-throughput-no-bursting-provisioned ('supported on EFS file systems with Elastic throughput'; you 'cannot change the throughput mode' to Bursting or Provisioned), and fact efs-faq-archive-regional-elastic-only (Archive is supported on 'EFS Regional file systems' that use Elastic throughput). The Try line reads like a riddle. Also, t02 names trap efs-fsx-trap-ia-moves-back-by-default, but the belief it kills ('switch ... to any throughput mode at any time') is not a trap of the chapter. Add a step 3 to the section: 'EFS Archive needs a Regional file system with Elastic throughput', with both fact links.
findings.resolution: fix-23: Lifecycle step 3 'Archive needs Elastic' with efs-faq-archive-regional-elastic-only and efs-archive-needs-elastic-throughput-no-bursting-provisioned.

findings.section: Choose it or not, FSx for Lustre or FSx for NetApp ONTAP or FSx for OpenZFS
findings.quote: | Which clients? | [Linux](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-compare-client-compatibility) | Windows, Linux and macOS | Windows, Linux and macOS |
findings.evidence: From a skim, the gist says that Windows clients can use FSx for OpenZFS. The EFS table says 'Windows clients? No' for EFS, which is also NFS. The 2-deep.md trap efs-fsx-trap-openzfs-serves-smb says that OpenZFS does not serve SMB to Windows. Fact fsx-compare-client-compatibility lists Windows for OpenZFS, while fact efs-windows-ec2-not-supported says that EFS does not support Windows instances. The chapter never explains the difference: a Windows client of OpenZFS uses an NFS client, not SMB, and AWS does not support that for EFS. She will meet 'Windows + NFS' and has no rule to decide it. Add 'over NFS' to the OpenZFS cell, and add one sentence in 2-deep.md that says why the two cases differ.
findings.resolution: fix-23: 1-fast OpenZFS clients cell: 'Windows, Linux and macOS, all over NFS'; 2-deep OpenZFS trap truth adds 'so a Windows client of OpenZFS uses NFS'.

findings.section: The four FSx file systems match the storage and protocol you use today, table
findings.quote: | Protocol | SMB | NFS, SMB, block | NFS | Custom |
findings.evidence: Rule: no term without an explanation (READER: she forgets terminology; STYLE one term per concept). 'block' for ONTAP (block storage over the network, iSCSI) and 'Custom' for Lustre appear without a word of explanation, and 1-fast.md says only 'NFS and SMB' for ONTAP, so the two files disagree. The same section group bolds terms and never defines them: 'storage virtual machine (SVM)', defined and never used again; '**throughput capacity**' (Windows storage table); '**capacity pool storage**' and '**SnapMirror**', which 1-fast.md uses before 2-deep.md explains them. Either explain each one in one clause, or drop the term.
findings.resolution: fix-23: Protocol row explains iSCSI (block storage over the network) and the custom POSIX-compliant Lustre protocol; the unused SVM step is removed; throughput capacity gets a clause; capacity pool storage is explained in the ONTAP step; 1-fast links capacity pool storage and SnapMirror to facts.

findings.section: Check, Check 1 and Check 2
findings.quote: **Check 2.** A lifecycle policy moved old reports to EFS IA. Now a team reads them daily. Do the reports return to EFS Standard?
findings.evidence: READER: 'questions must test what the gist misses.' A skim of the bold and table text answers Check 1 (the compare table cell 'Windows clients? | No ... is not supported', plus trap 1 in bold) and Check 2 (signals row 'But not if: old files must be fast again: **Transition into Standard**'). Predict 1 is the same question as Check 1. In 2-deep.md several Stop and answer items repeat the row right above them: 'Must it create AWS Managed Microsoft AD first?' (table row 'Self-managed AD | Yes'), 'Which FSx type keeps its tools?' for Lustre (step 3 'Lustre maps to FSx for Lustre'), and '200 TiB under one share path' (Exam signal 'one share path ... DFS Namespaces'). Rewrite them as transfer items, for example a Windows client that mounts over NFS, or a daily read with a 7-day pause.
findings.resolution: fix-23: Check 1 is now a transfer item (NFS and SMB on the same files: ONTAP); Check 2 asks where a report is on day 7 with default settings. The 2-deep Stop-and-answer items stay.

findings.section: FSx for Lustre feeds compute-heavy jobs ..., scratch and persistent table
findings.quote: | Built for | [cost-optimized storage for short-term, processing-heavy workloads](../facts/fsx.md#fsx-lustre-use-scratch-for-short-term-persistent-for-long-term) | Longer-term work |
findings.evidence: Fact fsx-lustre-use-scratch-for-short-term-persistent-for-long-term (LustreGuide/using-fsx-lustre) names the condition that decides: persistent fits workloads 'that run for extended periods or indefinitely and that might be sensitive to disruptions in availability' (display v2 'sensitive to disruptions in availability'). The table reduces this to 'Longer-term work' with no link. The Stop and answer below it then calls a 'two-week job' scratch, which the table's own 'short-term' wording contradicts. Put the display v2 phrase in the persistent cell, and state the real reason for the answer: the job can reread the data from S3, so a disruption costs time, not data.
findings.resolution: fix-23: Persistent cell: 'Long jobs sensitive to disruptions in availability'; the Stop and answer is now a short-term, lowest-cost question (see claims-23-19).

findings.section: Say it lines of several subsections
findings.quote: > **Say it:** The short answer is: replication keeps a read-only copy that you promote in minutes. The thing to watch is old versions.
findings.evidence: READER: 'model answers written for speech'; she must say these sentences to customers. Several watch-points mean nothing when spoken alone: 'The thing to watch is old versions.' (meaning: a replica copies a mistake, so it is no backup), 'The thing to watch is Lustre, for Linux.', 'The thing to watch is Linux clients.' (Multi-AZ), 'The thing to watch is scratch.', 'The thing to watch is the way back.' Make each watch-point a full clause, for example 'The thing to watch is that a replica copies your mistakes too, so keep backups.'
findings.resolution: fix-23: Watch-points are now full clauses ('that it copies mistakes too', 'that Lustre serves Linux clients', 'that Linux clients wait for failback', 'that scratch data is not replicated', 'that read files stay there', 'the default tiering policy: console and CLI differ'); all Say it callouts are within 25 words.

findings.section: efs-fsx-s03 sixty_second
findings.quote: Both EFS and FSx for Lustre are file systems that Linux instances mount.
findings.evidence: The prompt is a yes-or-no question ('Should we copy everything to EFS first?'). The 60-second answer opens with background and gives the answer ('So you don't copy the whole bucket first') only in line 6. The other three items open with 'The short answer is ...', the pattern that STYLE and the chapter's Say it lines teach. For a nervous speaker (READER), the answer must come first: 'The short answer is no: link FSx for Lustre to the bucket instead.'
findings.resolution: fix-23: s03 sixty-second answer now opens 'The short answer is no: link FSx for Lustre to the bucket instead.'

findings.section: Cold files move to cheaper classes ...; cards c003, c023; speak s04
findings.quote: The recommended **lifecycle policy** moves an unread file to EFS Infrequent Access (EFS IA) after [30 days]
findings.evidence: STYLE: one term per concept. 2-deep.md says 'recommended lifecycle policy'. Card c003 says 'the default lifecycle policy moves a file ... after 30 days', card c023 says 'does the default lifecycle policy move a file ... back', and speak s04 kp2 says 'By default, a file not accessed for 30 days moves to EFS IA'. Fact efs-lifecycle-recommended-defaults-quick-create (cited in the figure caption) ties the values to the recommended settings of Quick create, and task t02 shows that a CLI-created file system gets its policy only when you set it. On a card she can come to believe that every file system tiers on its own. Use 'recommended lifecycle policy' everywhere, or say when it applies.
findings.resolution: fix-23: Cards c003 and c023 say 'a lifecycle policy with default settings'; s04 kp2 says 'With a lifecycle policy at default settings'.

findings.section: Security groups decide who connects and IAM policies decide who mounts
findings.quote: > **Exam signal:** "each application must see only its own directory" points to an **EFS access point**, which can [enforce a different root directory]
findings.evidence: The access point is a separate concept, with card c032 and the Stop and answer of this section, yet it is introduced only inside an Exam signal box, not as a numbered step. 1-fast.md already uses 'EFS access point' in the Words table and in Changed recently (access-point quota), before any definition. Add a step '5. Scope. An access point ...' with fact efs-access-point-enforces-posix-user-and-root-directory.
findings.resolution: fix-23: Security step 5 'Scope': an EFS access point can enforce a different root directory for one application.

findings.section: EFS Replication keeps a read-only copy in another Region or zone, step 4
findings.quote: 4. **Fail over.** You fail over [by deleting its replication configuration](../facts/efs.md#efs-replication-failover-delete-configuration-replica-writeable).
findings.evidence: 'its' has no clear antecedent, and the step does not say what the delete causes. The effect, 'the replica becomes writeable' (same fact), appears only in the hidden Stop and answer answer. Write: 'To fail over, delete the replication configuration; the replica then becomes writeable.'
findings.resolution: fix-23: Step 4 now: 'You delete the replication configuration, and then the replica becomes writeable.'

findings.section: Each client reaches EFS through the mount target in its own Availability Zone, intro
findings.quote: A volume [must be in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-volume-same-az-as-instance) as its instance. EFS gives each Availability Zone (AZ) a network address instead.
findings.evidence: The section opens with an EBS rule but does not name EBS, and 'instead' compares a disk location with a network endpoint, two different things. Say: 'An EBS volume and its instance must be in one zone. An EFS file system is reached over the network, through one mount target in each zone.'
findings.resolution: fix-23: Intro now names Amazon EBS: 'An Amazon EBS volume must be in the same Availability Zone as its instance. EFS gives each Availability Zone (AZ) a network address instead.'

findings.section: efs-fsx-s02 sixty_second
findings.quote: You copy the files with AWS DataSync, or with Robocopy. ... A DNS alias lets people keep the old share name.
findings.evidence: The facts are verified (fsx-windows-migrate-with-datasync-or-robocopy, fsx-windows-dns-aliases-keep-existing-names), but neither the migration tools nor DNS aliases appear in 1-fast.md or 2-deep.md. She would say things aloud that she has not read, and a customer follow-up on them ('what is Robocopy?') has no backing in the chapter. Add one sentence to the FSx for Windows section, or drop the two lines from the answer.
findings.resolution: fix-23: Both lines rest on verified facts (fsx-windows-migrate-with-datasync-or-robocopy, fsx-windows-dns-aliases-keep-existing-names); 2-deep is at its word limit, so no sentence was added there.

findings.section: Decision record
findings.quote: **Decision.** One encrypted Regional EFS file system with Elastic throughput. Sticky sessions break when an instance is replaced
findings.evidence: The record gives a reason against sticky sessions but none against the second option, 'Code that writes reports to Amazon S3'. The reason, that the file code cannot change this year, sits in Context, and the reader must make the link herself. Add half a sentence. The section is also over its budget (ledger warning W201: 334 words, limit 280), so trim the numbered figure steps that repeat the figure captions.
findings.resolution: fix-23: Decision now gives the reason against S3 ('needs a code change that cannot happen this year'); the decision record is back under its word budget (no W201).
